thread.title: Why Apple Is Failing In China - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Early Retiree
title: Why Apple Is Failing In China - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
How much is Apple's China business worth? Rather unsurprisingly, the quick and easy reading of Tim Cook's disappointing letter to Apple ( AAPL ) investors was the market's interpretation. As Howard Marks says, the market's intelligence is rarely above average.
Tim Cook's letter basically seemed to imply that Apple's China business was cut in half in Q1/19. Since he blamed Greater China for "most of our revenue shortfall to our guidance, and over 100 percent of our year-over-year worldwide revenue decline" and the shortfall to Apple's guidance was $8B at its midpoint, while the YoY decline was $4B, we can estimate that China contributed at least $6B to the decline. This makes an annualized $24B and since China contributed $52B to total 2018 revenues , we get the ~50% cut. Finally, since China contributed 20% to Apple's 2018 overall revenues, if half of it falls away, the stock should fall 10% - right? This is what it did, but it is actually wrong.
First, we should not annualize the figure. Revenues from China varied enormously every quarter in 2018. A correct reading compares only Q1/18 to Q1/19 - i.e. $18B to (our estimated) $12B. So we are talking about a - still enormous - 33% decline.
Second - most importantly - not all revenues carry the same profit margins. We don't know for sure (Apple doesn't disclose margins), but in countries where Apple dominates, margins are probably higher and lower in those where it has to fight for attention, market share and needs to invest more for success. We also have to consider the ~$9-12B contribution from Alphabet ( GOOG ) in exchange for Google being the default search engine in the Apple world. This enormously increases profit margins for those countries where Google is used - which excludes China and makes the Chinese business much less valuable.
80% of Apple's total revenues include this $9-12B contribution, which falls directly to the EBT line.
Revenues excluding China (all figures in billions)

So there already is a 3.9% difference in net profit margins and the Chinese business is down to 16.8% instead of 20% of total business. Since larger businesses generally have higher operating leverage and specifically in China Apple is selling less additional services (iTunes, Apple Pay etc. are not very successful - see below), I guess that the actual net profit margin in China is around 15% at best. This would mean that its contribution to Apple's profits was only ~$7.8B in 2018 or 13% of net income. Now, if 30% of revenues go away, operating leverage shrinks even further, so let's cautiously assume Apple lost half of its Q1/18 China net income in Q1/19 and that this will continue through the entire year. Hence, for the full year, $3.9 of net income would be lost, representing 6.6% of total net income.
However, I'm not so sure the stock should therefore have lost 6.6% on Thursday instead of 10%, since Apple had been struggling in China for some time and a struggling, lower-margin business is not worth the same earnings multiple as a robust, market-leading, high-margin business.
Why Apple failed in China The short answer is WeChat .
Last week, also for political reasons, the ongoing trade war was frequently blamed for Apple's shortfall in China. My fellow contributor Paulo Santos even suggested Chinese consumers are boycotting Apple because of bad feelings towards the U.S. and its president.
But why would China boycott a phone which is largely made in China and prefer a Chinese brand, while both phones have U.S.-made operating systems? Why would the Chinese customer not boycott Android phones as well?
The fact is that for the Chinese, the operating system actually doesn't matter that much anyway, as they have WeChat, which is akin to another operating system layered on top of the phone's own one. WeChat is an extremely powerful platform which basically combines Facebook ( FB ), Youtube, WhatsApp, Spotify ( SPOT ), Paypal ( PYPL ), Netflix ( NFLX ) under one roof. You can chat, make payments, participate in work groups, do free video calls, shop, share files and large videos, hail cabs and much more.
Even on iPhones, WeChat takes over the home screen , so that free WeChat calls ring the phone just like any other call even while the phone is locked.
In China, everybody uses WeChat, which means about 1 billion users, and the average user spends over one hour every day on the platform. More importantly, about one third of its users spend 4 hours/day or more on this "Everything App".
The result is an enormous network effect and in China there is no such thing as an "Apple ecosystem" that locks in its users. When asked, which of the two they would drop if they had to, almost no Chinese user would drop WeChat , while keeping the iPhone. And with the huge success of WeChat Mini Programs, which were launched last year, apps as we know them from our phones have only become more obsolete. There are already thousands of these programs on every topic imaginable. You can buy gifts, make restaurant reservations, order coffee, play games, invest in financial products etc.
So China doesn't need to boycott any U.S. phone or operating system, as it simply uses them as the hardware and software necessary to run WeChat. In China, the iPhone is only an expensive luxury gadget. Users don't get locked in.
Unsurprisingly, phone makers in China mostly compete on price - and Apple has been struggling for a while already. One year ago, analysts predicted " another tough year" for the iPhone maker in China. And this was on Forbes, so the market was certainly aware of it. Today, Apple is only the fifth-biggest phone seller in China and its market share has stagnated for a while, while the four bigger domestic competitors have been growing in popularity. And since there aren't many additional services Apple can sell to its users in China, the usual argument about Apple's low market share, but high profit share, doesn't fit here. For services, music, video, apps, calls, messaging, books, news, payments there is WeChat. And this is very likely the only aspect of the story that originates in a clear political strategy. Which also means that China won't allow its customers to be locked into a U.S.-made ecosystem. Ever.
Bottom line We have seen that last year Apple likely made about $8B of net profit in China (at best) and the writing was already on the wall. There is no lock-in, no growing, recurring services revenues argument. It was pretty clear that China would continue to be a struggle, with lower margins, less certainties and strong competition backed by plain and simple protectionism. I think it is unlikely that these earnings were worth more than Samsung's ( OTC:SSNLF ), as Apple doesn't have much of a moat in China and probably only industry-average profit margins. Samsung currently trades for 6.4 times forward earnings and has a 2019e net profit margin of 15.7%. Even if we give Apple a bonus for its strong brand and appeal, it is unlikely that the market valued its Chinese net income at a multiple higher than 7-8x. So the entire Chinese market would have accounted only for ~$60B of market value before it was (at worst) cut in half by Cook's letter. But a $30B loss of value is just $6.35/share and not a $16 drop like the one we watched recently. And much of this should have already been priced in, since the market was only expecting bad news from Apple and had downsized its market valuation by a gigantic $350B - notably, before Thursday's additional $75B shrinkage.
At this point I guess that the risk/reward has changed to the buyers' favor and have established a long position in Apple for $144.
